artifacts.notes:
WHAT THIS IS: uncorrected optical character recognition of a whole 1862 Missal, 108,905 LF-terminated lines, valid UTF-8, no CR bytes, landed as a plain source artifact and nothing more. It is deliberately NOT structured as liturgical records, for the reason src/sources/inventories/lt-hist-rights-audit-v1.toml gives about the prior corpus's eight 'sections' over this same file: their only structural claim was a line range over the download, so a comparison of two of them compares the scanner's disagreements rather than the liturgy's. Addressability by identity, this collect of this Mass, belongs to passage records with real loci over these exact bytes. Until such a passage exists this artifact is a finding aid.

READ THE EDITION RECORD BEFORE CITING THIS TEXT. It is a commercial Ratisbon printing conformed to the Roman text, not a typical edition, and its appendix and its calendar of Masses granted for particular places are the publisher's compilation rather than the Roman book's contents.

THE GOOGLE QUESTION, DECIDED ON THE BYTES. This is a Google digitisation -- its fifth line OCRs as 'Digitized by Googl' and the stamp stands whole at line 79 -- which is why the fold-in of this book was held back from the three that went first. Two routes were offered: land a derivative with the Google matter removed by one stated replayable transformation, or register the scan remote and unresolved and hold no bytes. NEITHER WAS TAKEN, and the reason is a fact about this file.

  WHAT IS NOT HERE. Google's front-matter statement -- 'This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves', the 'Usage guidelines', 'About Google Book Search' -- is ABSENT. Searched case-insensitively over the whole 2,503,914 bytes: 'usage guidelines' 0, 'about this book' 0, 'books.google' 0, 'do not assume' 0, 'watermark' 0, 'non-commercial' 0, 'attribution' 0, 'creative commons' 0, 'all rights' 0, 'public domain' 0, and 'copyright' 0. Not one word of Google-authored prose is in this file, and no notice, licence, reservation or condition of any kind appears in it.

  WHAT IS HERE. The page-foot stamp alone: 546 lines contain the string 'google', and a wider sweep that also catches the mangled forms finds about 904 lines in 238 distinct spellings -- 'Digitized by Google' 470 times, then a bare 'Digitized by' 119 times where the word was cut off, 'Digitized by Googl', 'Digitized by GooqIc', 'Digitized by Goegle', 'kJ by Google', and two hundred more. Four words at the foot of a page. It states who ran the scanner, grants nothing and reserves nothing.

  WHY NOT ROUTE (a), THE DERIVATIVE. Because no single stated transformation removes the stamp, and the file is the proof. A strict pattern on 'Digitized by Google' leaves more than four hundred mangled forms behind, which would misrepresent the derivative as clean. A pattern loose enough to catch 'jitized by Google' and 'd by Google' also matches running Latin: the Ritus servandus and De defectibus are full of 'digiti', 'digitis' and 'digitorum' -- at lines 8751, 8968, 8972, 8975, 9085, 9285 and 9664, among others -- and deleting those lines would cut rubrics about the celebrant's fingers out of a Missal. The honest choices were a stated rule with a known large residue or an unstated hand-picked list, and the second is exactly what the offered route forbids.

  WHY NOT ROUTE (b), REMOTE AND UNRESOLVED. Because 'unresolved' would record a doubt these bytes disprove. The doubt was that a public-domain text had Google's own matter added to it; the search above shows it has not, beyond a four-word stamp with no claim in it.

  AND THE DISTINCTION IS CHECKABLE, NOT CONVENIENT. This repository already holds the contrasting case. `artifact.eugene-cummiskey.roman-missal-english-laity.philadelphia-1843.ia-djvu-ocr`, Internet Archive item romanmissaltran00englgoog, stands remote and unresolved for precisely this reason and earns it: its lines 1 to 65 are Google's front-matter block entire, 'Usage guidelines' at line 16 and 'About Google Book Search' at line 60 [verified 2026-08-01 on a fetched copy]. That item has the block and no page stamp; this one has the stamp and no block. Same test, opposite findings.

  THE STAMP IS RETAINED, deliberately. It carries no notice and no claim, so removing it buys nothing; it is the only page-boundary evidence in this text layer; and the Lasance fold-in already set the precedent by retaining the 'http://ccwatershed.org' stamp at the foot of every page of its scan. A reader must not mistake it for a rights notice, and must expect it interleaved through any quotation that spans a page break.

OCR QUALITY, AND IT IS THE BEST OF THE FIVE LATIN AND ENGLISH SCANS FOLDED IN FROM THIS CORPUS. Measured here by scripts/_ocr_quality.py at a Latin function-word share of 0.1792 over 357,261 tokens, English 0.033, classified `prose-latin` -- comfortably above the roughly ten per cent at which that tool says running Latin prose sits, and more than twice the 1570's and the 1604's. The reason is the type: this is a clean nineteenth-century roman face on machine paper, not sixteenth-century abbreviated printing. Whole paragraphs of the bulls, the rubrics and the Canon read straight through. The damage that remains is characteristic and not random: the printed accents on the Latin OCR as digits and punctuation ('mis6ric6rdiam', 'D6minum', 'devoti6ne'), so a search for an accented word will fail where the same word unaccented succeeds; running heads fuse to body text; and the tables, the calendar and the errata list -- which are set in small type and columns -- are wreckage. QUOTE FROM THIS ARTIFACT ONLY THROUGH A CHECKED PASSAGE. A negative raw-line search over the accented text establishes nothing, for the reason just given.

IDENTITY. The item was uploaded on 2014-12-01 by the Wikimedia Books Uploader bot from a Google scan of the New York Public Library's copy, in collection americana, 922 page images, creator 'Catholic Church', publisher 'Ratisbonae, sumtibus chartis et typis Friderici Pustet', LCCN 33036844, OCLC 7426908, page_number_confidence 84, and the item's PDF derivative is flagged `pdf_degraded = invalid-page-size`. The title page and the colophon were both read here and agree with the catalogue. One date in the back matter did NOT resolve and is recorded as unresolved rather than guessed: a conformity note above the colophon OCRs as 'Concordant cum Originalibus. RAtUbon» 31. HatL 1866.', where the year could be 1862 or 1866 and the month is illegible; nothing in this record depends on it, and it is written down so the next reader does not have to find it again.
artifacts.rights_basis: Public domain in the United States because the book was first published outside the United States before the pre-1931 line, and on that ground alone. THE LINE, AND THE YEAR IT WAS DERIVED FOR. Any work first published abroad before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart as current on 1 January 2026. THE LINE MOVES EVERY JANUARY, which guidance/missals.md:249 states in terms, so it is written here as derived for calendar year 2026 and not as a standing rule: on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932, and a later reader must re-derive it rather than quote this sentence. Publication at Ratisbon in 1862 clears the line by sixty-nine years, so the line would have to advance to 1863 -- not before 2095 at one year a January -- before it reached this book. AND RESTORATION CANNOT REACH IT EITHER. Restoration under 17 U.S.C. 104A grants a foreign work the remainder of the term it would have had, generally ninety-five years from publication; for 1862 that ran out at the close of 1957, so there was nothing left to restore on 1 January 1996, and the Holy See's Berne accession of 12 September 1935 and Bavaria's earlier adherence are alike beside the point. THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: the Internet Archive item's own metadata names the recogniser as ABBYY FineReader 9.0 with abbyy-to-hocr 1.1.11 and the page images as Google's -- scanner google, sponsor Google, google-id E7sPAAAAIAAJ, source books.google.com -- and whichever of the two parties ran the recogniser, it was a program and not a person, so there is no author to hold a right in the text layer. AND THE GOOGLE MATTER WAS LOOKED FOR IN THESE BYTES RATHER THAN ASSUMED FROM THE FIRST PAGE; SEE `notes`, WHICH RECORDS THE SEARCHES, WHAT THEY RETURNED, AND WHY NEITHER OF THE TWO ROUTES OFFERED FOR IT WAS TAKEN. In summary: Google's front-matter statement and its usage guidelines are NOT in this file, the only Google matter present is the four-word page-foot stamp Digitized by Google, that stamp carries no notice and reserves nothing, and it is retained rather than stripped for the reason the Lasance fold-in retained its scan host's watermark. THE BOOK'S OWN PRINTING PRIVILEGES ARE NOT A LIVE RIGHT EITHER. It reprints Clement VIII's and Urban VIII's prohibitions on unlicensed printing of the Missal and carries the Bishop of Ratisbon's licence to Pustet of 1 September 1861; those are ecclesiastical printing controls of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries, they were never United States copyright, and no party to them claims anything now. NOT RELIED ON, EXPRESSLY: that the Internet Archive item is available, that the download succeeded, or that any host marks the scan public domain. guidance/sources.md:395-400 holds that availability and successful download are insufficient for `tracked`, and the item's Public Domain Mark 1.0 was the whole of the prior lt-hist corpus's ground for this book -- the ground refused at src/sources/inventories/lt-hist-rights-audit-v1.toml. The mark is recorded as a fact about the item and is not a link in this basis.

edition.authority: NO PROMULGATING AUTHORITY OF ITS OWN. The authority this book carries is an approbation, not a promulgation, and the difference is the whole of why this record exists. Ignatius von Senestrey, Bishop of Ratisbon, subscribed letters at Ratisbon on 1 September 1861, printed in the book at lines 712 to 745 of the text layer, which recite that by the decrees of Clement VIII, Urban VIII and others no printer may publish the Roman Missal unless the conformity of the new edition with the Roman archetypes is plainly established and the licence to print it has been sought and obtained from the Ordinary of the place; that two priests were deputed at Frederick Pustet's petition to examine this hand-format edition; that they reported it conformed to the authentic Roman exemplars and that the additions and corrections prescribed by the Sacred Congregation of Rites on 26 September 1860 and by Pius IX on 27 September 1860 and 12 March 1861 had been inserted or noted; and that the bishop therefore approves it and grants licence to publish. That is a licence to print a book, granted by a local ordinary to a commercial firm. It is not an act of the Holy See imposing a text.

AUCTORITATE RECOGNITUM, then ACCURATISSIMA EDITIO CUM ADDITAMENTIS NOVISSIMIS, CUM APPROBATIONE SACRORUM RITUUM CONGREGATIONIS, and beneath that RATISBONAE, MDCCCLXII, SUMTIBUS CHARTIS ET TYPIS FRIDERICI PUSTET. The colophon after the appendix reads Ratisbonae: Ex Officina Fr. Pustet, S. Sedis Apostolicae Typographi. passages.notes:
WHAT THIS PASSAGE IS FOR. It is the public-domain antecedent witness for three
orations the 1962 typical edition reprints, and it is cited to show that their
wording is preexisting material of that edition under 17 U.S.C. 103(b), per
src/sources/inventories/missale-romanum-1962-facsimile-rights-v1.toml. It is
not a claim that the 1862 Pustet is a typical edition, and nothing about the
history of the rite is inferred from it here.

TWO LIMITS OF THE TEXT LAYER, RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER. First, the
`Secreta.` heading is absent: this book sets an ornamental initial on each
oration and the recogniser drops it, so the Secret opens as `/>|Onc6de` at line
50294 with its heading gone, and the Collect as `QUstridi.` at 50167. The
Secret is therefore identified by its position -- after the Offertory of this
formulary and before the `Alia Secrcta` pointer at line 50301 -- and by its
incipit, not by a printed heading in these bytes. Second, the printed stress
accents recognise as digits and punctuation throughout (`D6minum`, `perp6tua`,
`qusesumus`), which is the characteristic damage the artifact record describes;
the letters are legible through it and the accents are not evidence here.

A RUNNING HEAD FALLS INSIDE THE RANGE. Line 50236 reads `Dominica XV. post
Pentecosten.` and is a running head fused into the body text, not the start of
the next formulary, which begins at line 50324. The artifact record names that
fusion as a known behaviour of this scan. It sits between the Epistle and the
Gospel of the Fourteenth Sunday and touches none of the three orations.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. No page image of this book was read for this passage; the
loci are over the retained text layer. The three prayers are recorded as being
in print in 1862 in this wording, which is what the 103(b) argument needs. The
1962 edition's own readings, its pointing and its accents were established
separately on that edition's page images and are not taken from here.
